newsitem.title: UK: Polygram sees music industry recovery.
newsitem.headline: Polygram sees music industry recovery.

text.p: Polygram NV, one of the five global powers in the music business, said Wednesday profits fell 18 percent in 1996 but that it believed the industry was set to recover after sales stalled last year.

The music and film company, which took a charge of 114 million guilders ($61.4 million) for a previously announced reorganization of its music operations, said 1996 net income after taxes and special items fell to 608 million guilders ($327 million) from 741 million ($399 million) in 1995.
Sales grew 7 percent to 9.45 billion guilders ($5.08 billion) from 8.80 billion ($4.73 billion).
Levy said Polygram expected to resume earnings growth in 1997 but would not specify by how much.

"We do not believe the music business to be a mature industry," President Alain Levy told a news conference in London, adding that he believed sales could grow at an annual rate of more than 5 percent.

The company was also optimistic about its Polygram Filmed Entertainment unit, which this week won 14 Academy Award nominations for films such as "Fargo," "The Portrait of a Lady," "Sleepers" and "Trainspotting."
Levy said, however, that the unit would not make a profit in 1997 because of the costs of setting up a distribution operation in the United States and a move to bigger budget films.

In the music business, Polygram plans releases this year by U2, Elton John and Van Morrison. It is also revamping its Motown unit, moving the famous label's headquarters from Los Angeles to New York as it seeks to recreate its heyday of the 1960s and early 1970s.

Levy said the $40 billion global music market hit a plateau last year, when sales grew just 3 percent after several years of double-figure increases. But he said that he felt the problem was a shortage of good music releases rather than the end of a business cycle.
"I think the issue is an issue of creativity. The music makes the market," he said.
Polygram, Bertelsmann, Sony Music, EMI and Warner dominate the global music business, accounting for more than two-thirds of sales.
As part of the restructuring, Polygram said it was cutting about 550 jobs, an increase on the forecast of 400 job losses made when the move was announced in October.
Chief Financial Officer Jan Cook said the restructuring would pay off in two or three years as the staff cuts trim the annual wage bill by some 50 million guilders ($26.9 million).
The company is also reorganizing its European music distribution and marketing and restructuring its classical music division.
Polygram's stock is listed in Amsterdam and New York, with many of its senior executives based in London.
The company's American Depositary Receipts rose $3 to $47 in late morning trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
